Still, it gives students a steady start and helps them get the most out of their lessons.

questions.title: technology
questions.passage: Few innovations have reshaped the classroom as swiftly as artificial intelligence. Advocates argue that students should embrace AI tools wholeheartedly, and their reasoning is compelling. A well-designed chatbot can clarify a baffling concept in seconds, generate practice questions tailored to a learner's weaknesses, and offer feedback at any hour without a hint of impatience. Therefore, for those who lack access to private tutors, such technology can be a remarkable equalizer. Nevertheless, an uncritical dependence on these tools carries genuine risks. When learners outsource every difficult task to a machine, they may never cultivate the perseverance and analytical thinking that authentic understanding demands. Moreover, AI systems occasionally generate confident yet inaccurate answers, and a student who cannot evaluate such claims is easily misled. Critics therefore warn that convenience can quietly erode intellectual independence. However, abandoning these tools altogether would be equally shortsighted, for they are becoming inseparable from modern life. The wisest course, then, is balance. Students ought to treat AI as a capable assistant rather than a substitute for their own effort, verifying its output and reserving the hardest thinking for themselves.

Private tutors are no longer necessary now that AI chatbots exist.

questions.passage: Have you ever wondered why the Moon looks bigger when it sits near the horizon? Many people believe the Moon actually grows larger at that moment, but this is only an illusion created by our own minds. When the Moon hangs low in the sky, we see it next to trees, houses, and distant hills. These familiar objects give our brains a sense of scale, so the Moon appears huge by comparison. Hold a small coin at arm's length and cover the Moon near the horizon. Then try the same thing hours later. The coin hides the Moon equally well both times. Our eyes, it turns out, are easily fooled by clever surroundings.

Younger speakers, eager to mark their own identity, invent slang that older generations may resist at first and later adopt without thinking. questions.title: photography
questions.passage: Taking a good photo is about more than just pressing a button. The most important thing to understand is light, because it shapes the whole picture. When the sun is low in the early morning or late afternoon, the light is soft and warm. A photo taken at these times often looks gentle and pleasing to the eye. Strong midday light, on the other hand, can create hard shadows on a person's face. Where you stand also makes a big difference to your final picture. A simple trick is to keep your arms close to your body for support. With a little practice, anyone can learn to capture a clear and beautiful moment. In the end, patience and a good eye matter more than an expensive camera.
